name: Maximalists
overview: In its own best terms, the Maximalist program is popular sovereignty run through one elected man. The nation is its citizens and its borders; an election hands the president the whole executive; and the permanent government (independent agencies, career prosecutors, a Fed that sets money without answering to anyone, judges who stall removals) is an unelected usurpation to be broken. From that follow the acts: mass deportation (3,000 ICE arrests a day, Oct 6), prosecution of those they see as having weaponized the state against Trump, budget control that starves hostile agencies (Vought's $11B+ in halted projects, Oct 2025), a Fed Board that answers to the president, tariffs as economic sovereignty, and election enforcement as defense of a citizens-only vote. Vought calls it a 'post-constitutional moment' to be corrected; Bannon calls it deconstructing the administrative state; Miller frames it as the nation choosing who belongs. Abroad the doctrine is power, not restraint: Iran must give up its program first, Venezuela is a criminal state.

The interest layer keeps the program running. Most members hold posts that exist at Trump's pleasure (Blanche was his personal lawyer; Patel, Pirro, Pulte), so maximal loyalty is also job security, and each prosecution or referral doubles as an audition for the next post up (Miller and Pulte were floated for Wiles's job, Oct 15). Outside government, a funded pipeline carries the doctrine: Bradley Impact ($27.1M, 2022) and DonorsTrust ($21.3M, 2024) fund Miller's America First Legal; DonorsTrust also funds Howell's Oversight Project. Detention contractors profit from the targets: GEO paid Homan and Venturella before their jobs and gave $4.4M to MAGA Inc. The movement voices now counted here sell the same program to an audience: Bannon's War Room and a possible 2028 run, Loomer's access to Trump, Prince's bid for a privatized removal business.

Acts depart from words in three places. First, 'America First' restraint gives way to loyalty when Trump goes to war: Bannon warned the Iran war could break MAGA and still told CPAC 'people have to have his back' (Mar 27); Loomer branded critics a 'foreign influence operation' (Mar 3); only Prince, whose trade is ground work, dissents. Second, the doctrine of total presidential power bends to the president's own retreats: Trump pulled arrest decisions back to career officials in spring and said Miller 'sometimes goes too far' (Atlantic, May 11), and the faction regained ground only when Trump turned again (Jun 1, Oct 6). Third, the courts: Cook stayed 5-4, the Powell probe closed, both ballot suits lost by Nov 2, and a grand jury refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson (Oct 27).

Precedent (my reading): A. Mitchell Palmer's 1919-20 raids. An attorney general seeking the presidency used deportation and sedition cases against a 'Red' threat, until Labor's Louis Post cancelled most warrants, a federal court (Colyer v. Skeffington) condemned the methods, and his predicted May Day uprising never came; the drive collapsed with his 1920 bid. It breaks here: Palmer acted alone and against his ailing president's indifference, while the Maximalists hold several agencies at once, have a funded legal arm outside government, and act on the president's own orders, so their limit is Trump's mood and the courts, not a rival cabinet officer.
